leading_positions.synthesis: Three of eight members prefer base editing as their single-part configuration, and all three name the same trio (Liu, Komor, Gaudelli) with near-identical citation wording about programmable single-base conversion without double-strand cleavage. They share the mechanistic case (deaminase tethered to a Cas9 nickase; the adenine editor required an evolved TadA) and the same two open risks: the increment over the 2020 CRISPR prize and the unresolved Kondo/Nishida Target-AID priority question. They differ in emphasis: Brzezinski stresses breadth of support and first clinical use, Chabes argues the 2020 prize honoured cleavage and not base conversion, and Zou notes that a Liu-only prize is defensible and that trainee credit is a judgement call. Aili, Aqvist, Linke and Somfai list B006 only as an alternative.

Aili alone prefers targeted protein degradation (Crews, Deshaies, Handa), combining the engineered heterobifunctional degrader with the cereblon molecular-glue mechanism. It is named as an alternative by Brzezinski, Chabes, Aqvist, Somfai, Sparr and Zou, so its acceptability is wider than its single first-preference count. Open issues are that no heterobifunctional PROTAC is approved, and that Ciulli, Sakamoto, Kim and Gray are left out of a three-person configuration.

Aqvist alone prefers biomolecular phase separation (Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen) as a physical-chemical organizing principle of the cell. Brzezinski, Linke and Sparr list it as an alternative, while Aili doubts its maturity. Pappu and Mittag are excluded, and it is contested which cellular condensates are genuine liquids.

The chair's own configuration is nanopore sensing (Bayley, Deamer, Akeson). The chair is the only member preferring it and no other member lists it as an alternative, so it is the least cross-supported single preference; the chair flags attribution across five credited names and a possible bias toward the physics of the ionic-current principle.

Somfai alone prefers Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling (Buchwald, Hartwig) as the only established general synthetic method on the shortlist, with a clean two-person attribution. It is the only synthetic-methodology configuration. Its stated risks are overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize, the Kosugi/Migita tin-amide precedent and the field's frequent past recognition.

Sparr alone prefers ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cullis, Hope, Madden) as lipid self-assembly turned into a medicine with validated global impact. Aili lists it as an alternative. The attribution problem (Anderson, Langer, MacLachlan left out) and the overlap with the 2023 Medicine prize are unresolved.

areas_of_agreement: All eight members submitted a single-part, three-or-fewer-laureate configuration, and every configuration is drawn from the ten shortlisted candidacies.
Base editing (B006), protein degradation (B068) and phase separation (B056) recur across alternatives lists, so the members' acceptable sets overlap more than their first preferences do.
Every member names attribution as the main weakness of their own preferred candidate, and none claims that the preference is free of reservation.
No member discloses a specific conflict or requests recusal for any shortlisted candidate.
scientific_disputes: Whether base editing is a distinct chemical achievement or an engineering extension of the Cas9 platform honoured in 2020 (Brzezinski, Chabes and Zou raise it against their own choice; Aili reads the 2020 prize as a stronger obstacle).
Whether biomolecular phase separation is a settled physical-chemical principle or still a contested biology question about which in vivo condensates are true liquids (Aqvist, Aili, Sparr).
Whether Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is a distinct chemical problem or an increment on the 2010 cross-coupling prize (Somfai).
Whether ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a molecular design discovery or pharmaceutical formulation, and whether they belong to Chemistry or to the Medicine prize area (Sparr, Aili).
Whether nanopore sequencing is chemistry or an instrument and genomics story (Linke).
attribution_disputes: B006: Kondo and Nishida's independent Target-AID cytidine deaminase fusion is excluded by the Liu, Komor, Gaudelli trio; Zou also raises Liu alone versus a trio.
B068: Aili's three names include Handa, so Ciulli, Sakamoto, Kim and Gray are not in the three-person configuration, and the PROTAC and glue strands have different lineages.
B056: Aqvist's Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen trio leaves out Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar theory may be equally part of the chemistry.
B017: Sparr's Cullis, Hope, Madden trio leaves out Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan across six credited names.
B048: Five credited names (Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz, Bayley, Akeson) must be cut to three, and the roles of Kasianowicz's 1996 demonstration and Branton are open.
B032: Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work is a priority question against the Buchwald and Hartwig pair.
maturity_disputes: B006 is the youngest candidacy (2016-2017) with a short clinical record and unsettled off-target, bystander and delivery questions (Chabes, Zou, Brzezinski).
B068 has no approved heterobifunctional degrader yet, although cereblon-based glue drugs are approved (Aili, Sparr).
B056 is contested on which cellular condensates are genuine liquids and on uneven links to function (Aqvist, Aili, Sparr, Linke).
B032 and B017 are mature with long independent confirmation, and the dispute for them is novelty and category and not maturity.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Brzezinski (Secretary) and Zou are Stockholm University colleagues, which both state is not a conflict with any candidate.
Linke, Somfai and Sparr share Lund affiliation, which is a connection among committee colleagues and not to any candidate.
Aili and Sparr disclose a research-field overlap on self-assembly, and Aili discloses a translational and biosensor-company background, with no tie to B006, B017 or B068 names.

Linke (nanophysics and molecular motors) and Aqvist (quantitative simulation) disclose field-based bias toward the ionic-current principle and toward quantitatively testable results respectively; no member requests recusal.
questions_for_round2: Is base editing (B006) a sufficient increment over the 2020 CRISPR-Cas9 prize, given that the 2020 citation concerned guided double-strand cleavage?
If B006 advances, should Kondo and Nishida (Target-AID) be included, replaced against Komor or Gaudelli, or left out, and can a three-person limit be defended?

Is the absence of an approved heterobifunctional PROTAC disqualifying for B068, or do clinical-stage degraders and the approved cereblon glue lineage suffice, and should the third name be Handa or Ciulli?
Is the in vivo status of condensates a disqualifying maturity issue for B056, or a normal open question, and can a Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen trio be defended against Pappu and Mittag?

Would the committee prefer a single achievement or a two-part prize, and if two parts, which pairings (for example base editing with a mature mechanism-based candidacy, or two degrader strands) avoid a person-count conflict?

For B017 and B048, can the credited names be cut to a defensible three and a citation written that a broad audience understands, and do members see these as chemistry and not Medicine or instrumentation?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows a plurality but not a majority: B006 has three explicit supporters, five other candidacies have one each, and majority is five. The other configurations share the same difficulty, which is that a credible three-person cut or a citation boundary must be defended against specific named exclusions. Round 2 should test whether support can consolidate around any configuration, using only positions stated in the eight round-1 files.
